# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden and a Halden Subset

This is the most decisive document in the set. It does what the meta-analysis said was needed: within-study tracking over time, a stricter hours measure, and a registered mediation test. It settles the two largest open questions reasonably well:
- **Durability.** The per-hour gain persists at 24 months, smaller than at nine months but clearly above zero.
- **Pure artifact.** The claim that nothing remains after correction is refuted for discretionary work.

Its weaknesses are mostly in how strongly it states things. It overstates the decline in one place and the mediation result in another. It also doesn't reckon with a contaminated control group or with the fact that its "confirmation" reuses the units that generated the hypothesis. The authors are partly defending their own earlier work, which is reasonable, but the framing occasionally shows it.

## Arithmetic check

Nearly everything reconciles:
- **Per hour, timesheets:** 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%.
- **Per hour, logs:** 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8 / 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Meetings:** treated −3.5 h versus control −0.2 h gives a 3.3 h difference, the same as the month-six exploratory figure.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter staffing:** restoring output after a −11.4% per-FTE fall needs about 1 / 0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, close to the county's 12%. A 9% cost rise fits labour being roughly three-quarters of cost per contact.

Three points need care.

**1. The summary mixes hours measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". The 12.5% is a timesheet figure, and logs didn't exist at nine months. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" matches the timesheet comparison (−22%), so the summary is inconsistent with the paper's own text.

**2. The decline isn't statistically established.** The confidence intervals overlap almost entirely: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months and +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. "The gain has therefore declined" states more than the data show. No test of the difference is reported.

**3. Control-office meeting figures need checking.** Two control offices cut meetings from 7.1 to 5.0 hours, a fall of 2.1 h each. Yet the control average moved only from 7.2 to 7.0. Assuming roughly equal weighting, the other five offices must have risen by about 0.5 h each, or the two audit offices drifted back up by month 24. This may be fine, but it should be shown with office-level data.

## Strengths

- **A stricter hours measure.** Log-in time is used alongside timesheets. Logs show slightly more treated-office work than timesheets (−11% versus −12%), which confirms that some unclaimed work existed, though not much.
- **A registered mediation plan.** It was filed at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes, with pre-specified mediators and a single outcome.
- **A genuine test of decay within the same trial.** This fixes the between-study weakness in the meta-analysis.
- **A direct check of the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies.** All four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which confirms that their "no decay" result couldn't speak to novelty.
- **Candour on the Halden subset.** "Survivors twice over" and "an upper bound" are the right framing.
- **Reporting an awkward observation.** The control-office meeting audit cuts against a pure "the hours cut causes it" story, and the authors report it anyway.
- **Consistent findings.** The coverage-bound arm was ended because of waiting times, which fits every earlier source.

## Problems

### 1. The mediation "confirmation" is not an independent replication

The registered test uses the same seven treated offices whose month-six data first suggested the meetings hypothesis. Later months are new observations, but the clusters are the same. Office-specific features that produced the original correlation, such as a manager who cut meetings and also drove output, will carry forward.

"A larger sample of office-months" adds little independent information. The effective sample is still 7 versus 7 clusters, and the confidence intervals (28–66%) may be too narrow if office-months were treated as independent. The paper doesn't say how clustering was handled in the mediation model.

The paper says this is a registered confirmatory test on the original units. Its language is stronger: the summary says it "confirms" the mechanism, and the analysis "survives" a test. A fair reading is "consistent with, under a registered model", not "confirmed".

### 2. The meetings share is partly an accounting identity

If meeting time counts as working hours and produces no recorded cases, then cutting meetings raises cases per hour almost by definition. That makes 47% largely a statement that meetings weren't counted as output. It doesn't show that the meetings were valueless. Their benefits, such as coordination, training and quality control, may sit outside the output measure.

Two details sharpen this:
- **What do the logs measure?** The paper describes logs as time staff spend "working on cases". If logs exclude meeting time, then output per log-hour wouldn't mechanically rise when meetings are cut. Why meetings mediate gains in that outcome then needs explaining. If logs include meeting time, the identity point applies. The paper should state which.
- **Quality is drifting slightly.** Appeal overturns moved from 3.1% v 3.0% to 3.2% v 3.0%. That is probably noise, but it is the one measure where meeting value would show, and it isn't moving the right way.

### 3. Other mediation weaknesses

- **Causal ordering is unaddressed.** Fewer meetings may reduce fatigue, so the 47% / 18% split depends on how the two mediators are ordered.
- **Confounding is admitted but not probed.** The authors acknowledge the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption but run no sensitivity analysis, such as an E-value or ρ-sensitivity bounds.
- **The fatigue pathway barely clears zero.** Its interval runs from 2% to 34%.

### 4. The control group was contaminated, and the paper doesn't account for it

From month 15, two of seven control offices adopted part of the treatment mechanism. That likely **biases the 24-month estimate toward zero**. Some of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% could be the control group improving, not the treatment effect fading. An analysis excluding those two offices, or a sensitivity check, should be reported.

The audit offices' +4.1% is itself an uncontrolled before-after comparison of self-selected offices. The obvious benchmark, the other five control offices over the same period, isn't reported.

### 5. Novelty versus a contingent perk

At 24 months, the novelty argument is substantially weakened. But treated staff knew they were in a trial and could lose the schedule. Working harder to keep a benefit is not the same as novelty, and it might fade once the schedule became permanent policy. Because of the difference-in-differences design, general observation effects apply to both arms. This motive applies only to the treated offices.

### 6. Problems with the Halden subset

- **Non-response is selective.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, from a pool already selected for having records, from survivors of a pilot with misreported attrition. Non-responders plausibly did worse.
- **No secular adjustment.** Output is compared with a baseline about 2.5 years earlier, with no comparison group, so general productivity growth inflates the result.
- **The baseline hours figure may not match the subset.** The 40.3 h baseline matches the 27-organisation time-tracking figure in Varga & Holm, not necessarily these 11 organisations.
- **The reversion story is stretched.** The summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency cited **client deadlines**, which is pressure in discretionary work, not presence-bound coverage. That reversion is evidence that discretionary work also has limits, and the framing blurs it.
- **Authorship.** Okafor is a co-author and was also an author of the original Halden paper, which misdescribed attrition. That isn't disqualifying, but it is relevant to how much weight to give unaudited subset data. The authors' "upper bound" caveat is appropriate.

### 7. Smaller points

- **Output per FTE is drifting down.** It went from −2.1% to −3.4%, and the interval now reaches −8%. With full pay maintained, cost per case closed is rising. Cost-effectiveness is still unreported for case-processing.
- **The sick-day measure is unchanged.** It is still not normalised per scheduled day, so the −27% likely overstates the health effect.
- **Single employer, public sector.** This is acknowledged.

## Bearing on earlier claims

| Claim | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Halden: +23% per hour, sector-general | **Refuted** on both counts |
| Varga & Holm: gains entirely an artifact, meetings is post hoc | **Not supported.** About 8.5% persists at 24 months under their own recommended standards. Their measurement critiques stand. |
| Meta-analysis: no decay, novelty set aside | **Overstated.** The long-run studies were all uncontrolled. Modest fading is possible but not statistically shown. |
| Meta-analysis: about 9–10% per-hour gain in discretionary work | **Corroborated** (8.5–9.8% at 24 months) |
| Coverage-bound work loses output | **Strongly corroborated.** The arm was ended at month 12, and restoring service would cost about 9% more per contact. |

## Current state of the evidence

| Question | Best reading | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | **About +8–10%**, persisting to 24 months, possibly faded from about 12% | Moderate to high, but from one randomised trial plus observational support |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | **About −2 to −4%**, cannot rule out −8% | Moderate |
| Cost per unit of output, discretionary work | Probably higher (full pay, slightly lower output). Not measured. | Low |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker about −10%. Restoring service costs about 9–13% more. | High |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the leading candidate, with fatigue secondary and a third unexplained. Part of the meetings share is definitional. | Low to moderate |
| Gains without cutting hours? | Hinted at by two contaminated control offices. **Untested.** | Low |
| Beyond 24 months, or private-sector discretionary work | Unknown | — |

## Bottom line

The debate across these five documents has converged on a defensible position. In discretionary work, a shorter week produces a moderate, durable gain in output per actual hour, roughly 8–10%. It is not large enough to fully offset the hours lost, and it appears to come substantially from removing low-value meeting time rather than from rest alone. In coverage-bound work, it reduces output and service.

The most important unanswered question is the one this report raises itself: whether a reorganisation arm, cutting meetings while keeping hours unchanged, would capture most of the gain without the hours cut. A three-arm trial would answer it.
